label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.

findings.quote: made deck's programme of experiments the team's queue
findings.why: Deck and its programme of experiments are named before a first reader knows what either is, so the opening paragraph of the hour is a stall.

findings.quote: had carried other sites' data in with them
findings.why: As a writer who is exacting about sources I want to know what kind of data leaked, and the chapter says only that it was 'other sites' data'.

findings.quote: redaction does not reach a commit already pushed
findings.why: The late review is told by the researcher at line 31, again here, and again at line 155, so the lesson is said three times.

findings.quote: Not from memory, and not from what anyone said. From the files.
findings.why: Three fragments in a row where one sentence could carry the thought, and the conductor repeats it in the next line.

findings.quote: It is the first sign in the record of members pacing each other
findings.why: The narrator reports from the record with no 'I' and no hindsight, where the editor could say what he made of it.

findings.quote: A check after the push finds what has already gone out.
findings.why: Restates the first failure's lesson from line 33 instead of letting the two scenes stand side by side.

findings.quote: Not one step said stop all day.
findings.why: Three plans were sent back, yet this sentence sounds like a reviewer that never refused, which is my rubber-stamp worry; it needs the count of stops set against it.

findings.quote: Studio would not. It asked me.
findings.why: The refusal and the question to the editor are told in Studio's own line at 59 and then again, with the same words, in the narrator's summary.

findings.quote: Part one was final and not yet locked. The lock tool existed.
findings.why: A run of five short sentences closes the chapter in a list of facts, and the 'Part one' and 'lock' it summarises have barely been explained.

findings.quote: You do not need my nine. You need one.
findings.why: 'My nine' is never spelled out here, so a reader arriving at the last chapter has to guess which nine are meant.

findings.quote: Everything I had to invent, or carry over by hand, is already there for you
findings.why: A strong claim with no source beside it, and unsourced claims are what I would not trust in a newsroom.

findings.quote: Add a second agent only when the first is busy.
findings.why: The bold step is about a second agent but the text under it is mostly about working with other people, and I lost which one the step is.

findings.quote: A brief and rules in plain words. A check every change passes.
findings.why: Seven fragments in a row recite the five steps again, one after another.

findings.quote: But build it the same way, and then do it again.
findings.why: 'Then do it again' closes step 4, this paragraph and the bold last line, so the same instruction lands three times.

what_holds: 08-hours-four-and-five-before-dawn.md: two failures kept in at full size, each with a rule, and the researcher's own line 'A review that runs after the push is a review that runs late' is exactly the kind of control I want to see.

15-hour-eighteen-faster-than-the-clock.md: the brakes held under a deadline, with three plans sent back, and Studio refusing a relayed word makes the editor's signature a real control rather than a stamp.

23-principles-and-build-your-own.md: the newsroom's first-agent page of rules (check numbers against sources, write only the claims register, stop before marking a claim as holding without a captured source) is something I would start with tomorrow.
notes: Role I would start with tomorrow: the researcher who checks every number against its source, with me signing. Where I would not trust it: reviews that run after the push (chapter 8) and any 'no step said stop' count without the number of stops beside it. None of the Principle 6 phrases were found in these three sections.
